Tandem / Group Meeting

Move fast, stay aligned.

We want to say less to the agent, yet expect the software to work exactly as we mean. How can we close that intent gap without giving up the fast start?

Preserve the fast start Keep intent aligned Reduce coordination effort
Group meeting opening

Opening: give the audience a moment to read the headline.

Today I want to introduce Tandem, starting with a tension that many of us experience when working with code agents. We want to move fast. That means we do not want to spend a long time explaining every detail before the agent starts. But when we see the result, we still expect it to behave exactly as we had in mind.

In other words, we want to say less and expect more. That is the attraction of these tools, but it also contains a contradiction: the less we explain, the more the agent must infer. Some of those inferences will be useful. Others may be reasonable, but different from what we intended.

By intent, I mean the outcomes, constraints, and tradeoffs the user cares about. Some are explicit. Some feel so obvious to the user that they never think to mention them. Others only become clear after trying an early version.

The tandem bicycle is a useful metaphor: the human and the agent contribute different things, but they need to move in a shared direction. We are not proposing perfect mind-reading, or asking users to write everything down before they can begin. The question is whether we can make discovering and preserving that shared direction less work, without losing the fast start.

The question this work explores In the vibe coding era, how do we ensure the code agent builds what the user actually expects?
Code agents today

Start with the alignment question, then trace the short request, visible activity, and reported test results.

We start from one question: in the vibe coding era, how do we ensure the code agent builds what the user actually expects? Before discussing specifications or a workflow, we need to understand this problem from the user's side.

A very natural way to work today is to type something like, "Add account deletion." The agent may inspect the repository, make a plan, change the interface and backend, write tests, and fix errors. That is an enormous amount of work from a very small amount of input.

And this is genuinely useful. Someone with no programming experience can ask for a personal task manager and get something that meets their needs. I do not want to argue that this way of working is wrong, or that everyone needs an additional process.

But look at the activity window. It shows a lot happening. It does not necessarily answer the questions the user cares about: What behavior did the agent choose? What did it assume? Which decisions need my input? Does this match what I meant? Visible activity is not the same as visible alignment.

This is the distinction highlighted on the left: easy to start, harder to know it's right. Ordinary language makes software creation accessible, but getting something that runs does not by itself tell the user that it does what they meant.

Then the agent announces that dozens or even hundreds of unit tests passed. That sounds reassuring, but as a user I still need to ask: did it do the right thing? Passing unit tests provide useful evidence about the behavior they exercise. The number alone does not tell me whether the expected outcomes match mine, or whether my complete user flow works.

If the agent misunderstood the request, that misunderstanding can appear in both the code and its tests. They can agree with each other without agreeing with the user. This is not an argument against unit tests; it is a distinction between passing checks and establishing that the software does what I wanted.

So the question at the bottom is not whether an agent can produce code or pass tests. It is whether we can trust the resulting behavior to match the user's expectations. How to capture and maintain those expectations comes next.

Transition: Account deletion gives us a small example of why working code, by itself, does not answer that question.

The intent gap / A concrete example

Working code can still implement the wrong intent.

Compact user request "Add account deletion."
Agent: Immediate purge Erases all records & blocks access immediately.
User: 30-day soft delete Blocks access but permits account restoration for 30 days.
Each can pass its own tests. Tests encode expectations too. If code and tests share the wrong assumption, passing them does not establish agreement with the user.

Four knowledge categories, from the user's perspective — not four regions of the circles.

KK / Known knowns
What I explicitly tell the agent.
KU / Known unknowns
What I know I still need to figure out.
UK / Unknown knowns
What I take for granted or recognize when I see it.
UU / Unknown unknowns
What I have not considered at all.

Reference: Thariq Shihipar, Anthropic — Finding your unknowns.

Intent gap / Simplified mental model

Use the circles as a simplified mental model, then briefly distinguish the four user-perspective categories below.

The user and the agent both bring defaults to a request. The user brings product context, team practices, and personal expectations. The agent brings repository patterns, learned conventions, and whatever it can infer from the prompt.

There may be a large overlap. That overlap is one reason a short prompt can work so well. But a single important difference can matter more than many correct assumptions. The circles here are illustrative, not a measurement of how often an agent understands a user.

Take "Add account deletion." In this example, the user is thinking: block normal access immediately, but give someone a chance to recover an accidentally deleted account. The agent might instead interpret deletion as immediately and permanently removing all records. At this point, these are different interpretations, not a confirmed specification.

Both implementations can be internally coherent. More importantly, each could pass tests written for its own interpretation. A purge implementation can pass tests that expect purge. A recovery implementation can pass tests that expect recovery. That does not mean the same correctly specified test would accept both.

This is not an argument against testing. It is a question about whose expectations the tests encode. If the code and the tests come from the same mistaken assumption, agreement between them does not establish agreement with the user. We need a way to make the important expectation explicit and carry it forward.

The circles are a simplified mental model, not a complete classification of what the user or agent knows. Our original reference is Thariq Shihipar's Anthropic article, Finding your unknowns. It offers a broader four-part lens from the perspective of the person asking the agent for help.

Known knowns, or KK, are what I explicitly tell the agent. Known unknowns, or KU, are questions I know I have not answered. Unknown knowns, or UK, are expectations I take for granted or recognize when I see them, but have not articulated. Unknown unknowns, or UU, are things I have not considered at all.

For example, "Add account deletion" is explicit input. If I know I have not chosen a recovery period, that is a known unknown. If I silently assume deletion can be undone, that may be an unknown known. A retention obligation I have never considered would be an unknown unknown; once it is raised, it becomes a question I know needs an answer. The category depends on what this user knows at this point, not on the topic alone.

These categories are not four regions of our two-circle picture, and unknown knowns do not mean facts known only to the agent. The article connects prototyping to recognizing and articulating tacit expectations, and blind-spot exploration to discovering issues we did not know to ask about. Neither approach guarantees that every unknown will be found.

Transition: A specification can capture that agreement. But when do we create the first specification: before building, or after we have already started?

Two common starting paths / Both need explicit intent

Spec first, or build first?

1. Spec-first

Comprehensive specification → first line of code.

Express intent before implementation. Upfront specification takes effort; real use can still reveal missing expectations.

2. Agent-first / Tandem's starting point

Request → try what the agent builds → refine expectations.

Vibe coding makes this a natural starting point. Learn through experience rather than write a comprehensive spec upfront.
Tandem embraces the fast start, then makes the agreement explicit. What the agent built is not automatically what the user wanted.

Spec: requirements and design expressed through text, diagrams, flows, or examples — not necessarily one document.

How do we turn a fast start into software that stays aligned with the user?

Two starting paths

Contrast the two paths, emphasize agent-first, clarify what "spec" means, then end with the bridge question.

There are two common starting points worth distinguishing. These are not the only ways to develop software, and real projects can mix them.

In the spec-first path, we aim to describe the intended system comprehensively before writing the first line of code. This makes the agreement explicit early, but it asks for substantial thinking and writing upfront. Even then, trying the software can reveal expectations that the initial specification missed.

In the agent-first path, we ask the agent to build before we have the first version of the spec. Powerful code agents make this attractive: seeing something run can be faster and more informative than describing it abstractly. But the output is not automatically an agreement. Simply documenting whatever the agent happened to build would preserve its assumptions, including the wrong ones.

Vibe coding makes agent-first a natural starting point. Start with a request, try what the agent builds, and refine expectations through experience rather than write a comprehensive spec upfront. This explains its appeal; it is not a claim that we have measured what most people prefer.

Tandem embraces that fast start. The challenge is turning what we discover into an explicit agreement, not treating whatever the agent built as what the user wanted. Spec-first remains a valid path, but agent-first is the starting point we focus on here.

Here, "spec" is shorthand for the artifacts that clearly convey requirements and design, not a prescribed document format. It can combine text, diagrams, flows, and examples: different views that make the same agreement understandable.

Enter with an agreed spec from Stage 1 or an existing project. Confirm scope and gaps.

Less writing upfront; less re-explaining later.

Intent lifecycle

Follow Stage 1, then trace Stage 2's single loop through user Attention and back to the agreed spec.

This is the central proposal: prototype to a spec, then build against it. Tandem is an optional layer above existing code agents, not a replacement coding model. The agent still supplies the ability to explore, implement, and run checks.

This is an exploratory first step toward guided development rather than freestyle agent use. We do not yet know whether this approach makes sense as a whole, or whether only some parts will prove useful. The purpose is to make a possible direction concrete enough to discuss, challenge, and learn from, not to prescribe a settled development method. Freestyle use remains a valid choice.

Stage 1 aims to reach the first agreed specification faster. Start with the user's statements, ask the consequential questions needed for a useful first prototype, then let the user play with it. New expectations return us to clarification and confirmation as we refine the prototype and agreement together.

The output is not a transcript of every conversation or a description of every prototype behavior. It is a synthesized first spec: what we intend, what scope we have agreed, and which assumptions or decisions remain open. The prototype helps discovery; it is not automatically the intended product or production-ready code.

Stage 2 is iterative, not a left-to-right process that runs once. Start with the agreed specification, implement and validate the affected use cases, then review the result. Review checks consistency and surfaces impactful issues requiring user judgment. One return path brings both drift and consequential issues to user Attention and decision.

Bring review findings to user Attention and record the decision before resuming affected work. Return to the agreed spec: correct code against it when the agreement still stands, or update and confirm it first when intent changes. Then implement, rerun the affected use cases, and review again. The spec remains the anchor throughout the loop, rather than being a document we leave behind at the start.

A satisfactory review can close the current change; the next change enters the same loop. This is not endless iteration or automatic rewriting of the specification after every review. We repeat when a correction, decision, or new change requires it.

An existing agreed spec can enter the second stage directly, after checking its scope and gaps. Existing code without an agreed account of its intended behavior is different: having a repository does not eliminate the need to clarify intent.

The hoped-for benefit is less writing upfront and less repeated coordination later. That is a hypothesis to evaluate, not a measured speed claim. It still requires user interaction; the question is whether that interaction prevents more effort and rework than it adds.

Stage 1 / Optimize time to the first agreed spec

Reach the first agreed spec. FAST.

Any code agent can prototype and ask questions. Tandem's goal: shorten the path from a rough idea to an explicit agreement.

Start: statements → Q&A → prototype play Account deletion example

Start with the goal

A short spoken or typed story reveals the goal behind “delete.”

"Sometimes people delete by mistake. They should have time to come back."
02 · Q&A

Clarify what matters first

Tandem asks: “Block normal access now, but allow recovery for 30 days?”

User: “Yes. At 30 days, recovery must end.” Enough direction to try a prototype.

Try recovery. Discover expectations that words alone did not reveal.

User looks for a deadline and Undo. Record this clue as OBS-01, not an agreed requirement.
Play reveals more? Return to Q&A and confirm. Faster agreement is the goal, not a measured result.
Recovery / REC-01
First spec / Agreed scope
Confirmed goal Let users recover from accidental deletion.
Agreed policy Block normal access now. Recovery allowed before 30 days; rejected at and after.
Open question Which legal records and shared assets must survive permanent purge?
OBS-01 / Pending Show the deadline and Undo? Awaiting user confirmation.
Prototype-led spec discovery

Emphasize FAST. Start with statements, then targeted Q&A, then prototype play. Return to clarification when play reveals more.

The key word on this slide is fast. Any capable code agent can build a prototype, ask questions, and write a specification. Those activities alone are not our contribution. Tandem's proposed value is shortening the path from a rough idea to the first agreed specification, with less user effort.

That means asking questions whose answers materially affect the first prototype, then prototyping just enough to learn, and capturing confirmed answers without making the user repeatedly explain them. We are optimizing the whole discovery loop, not the number of screens or lines of code generated. We should measure time and user effort to an agreed spec, alongside missed expectations and later rework. We have not established a measured speed advantage yet.

We begin with the reason behind the request. The user says, "Sometimes people delete by mistake. They should have time to come back." That gives us a goal: recovery from accidental deletion. It does not yet give us a precise duration, access policy, or interface design.

Next comes targeted Q&A, before prototype play. Tandem asks whether normal access should stop immediately while recovery remains possible for 30 days. The user confirms and makes the boundary explicit: at 30 days, recovery ends. We can capture REC-01: recovery is allowed strictly before deletion time plus 30 days, and rejected at and after that deadline. The duration is a proposal until the user confirms it, not an invented requirement.

We do not need exhaustive questioning or a long requirements document first. Resolve the consequential choices needed for a useful first prototype, then let the user play with that recovery flow. The prototype makes the agreed direction tangible while leaving room to discover missing expectations.

While trying the prototype, the user looks for a deadline and an Undo action. That is useful evidence about what might matter to them. We record it as OBS-01. But an observation is not yet a confirmed requirement: perhaps the user expects Undo, perhaps they only want to know whether recovery is possible. We should ask rather than silently turn the observation into a feature.

These discoveries send us back to focused Q&A and confirmation. Statements, Q&A, and prototype play describe the starting order, not a one-pass process. The first agreed spec combines confirmed answers with explicitly open questions.

On the right, notice what the first spec includes and what it does not claim. The recovery goal and policy are agreed. The deadline-display and Undo experience still need confirmation. Legal retention and shared-asset treatment also remain unresolved, so permanent purge cannot proceed on an invented default.

This is enough to anchor the confirmed recovery scope, not enough to call the entire deletion feature settled. The interaction can repeat where needed. Prototype code may later be reused, revised, or replaced. Its value here is helping the user reveal intent, not making every implemented behavior authoritative.

This is a concrete example of the first-stage experience in Tandem. It is a different project from the account-deletion example: the request here is to build a navigatable 3D app for a Tesla Model Y. The important point is how a short idea becomes something the user can inspect.

In the center, the prototype shows a vehicle with camera and orbit controls. Instead of asking the user to describe every interaction abstractly, we give them an experience to react to. They can discover whether the available views match what they meant, which controls feel missing, and what needs clarification. Those are questions the prototype can help uncover, not answers we should assume from looking at the screenshot.

The feedback area provides a place to describe changes, while the artifact list includes a draft feature specification. This illustrates the intended relationship: experience, feedback, and the emerging agreement remain close together. The aim is not simply to generate a visual result; it is to help the user express expectations that were difficult to state upfront.

The screenshot shows Design active and the earlier prototype retained for review. Our two presentation stages are broader than the individual tabs in the application. We are using this screen to illustrate the prototype output and its handoff, not claiming that the application is still editing it in its Prototype stage. The capture does not demonstrate that every visible control works or that all requirements have been accepted.

This is the limit of the evidence: a prototype makes an idea tangible, but its behavior is not automatically agreed intent or production-ready software. The user must still confirm what should be preserved, changed, or left open. That is what turns an early experience into a useful first specification.

Spec-anchored development

Start with the understandable agreement on the left. Emphasize the two core commitments on the right; distinguish the evolving supporting direction beneath them.

The phrase I want to emphasize is one shared intent, different views. By specification, we do not mean that the user must consume a huge document. We mean an agreement that can be expressed through a linked set of understandable artifacts. These are not separate specs that can each invent their own policy.

Here, the flow shows what the user does and what the system does: deletion blocks normal access immediately, followed by a possible recovery request. The timeline makes the boundary easy to inspect: allow recovery before 30 days; reject it at and after the deadline. The decision map shows why permanent purge is still blocked. Each view makes a different aspect easier to understand, while keeping agreed behavior separate from unanswered questions.

The future direction is to generate the useful views dynamically for the project, rather than impose one fixed diagram set. A GUI may benefit from screens and interaction flows. A CLI may need command journeys and output examples. A service may need request sequences and contracts. This is a direction we want to pursue, not a claim that adaptive artifact generation is already complete.

On the right are two core commitments, rather than a generic implement-test-review sequence that an existing code agent can already perform. First, keep the agreement authoritative. Second, bring consequential decisions back to the user. The left makes the agreement understandable; the right describes how that agreement governs development.

The first commitment has two safeguards: spec changes before code changes, and post-implementation review. When requirements or design change, update the affected specification and confirm the agreement before implementation. The spec guides the code; it is not written afterward merely to describe what the agent happened to build.

Post-implementation review serves both core commitments, with two distinct purposes. Check consistency: do the actual code and use-case evidence match what was agreed? Also bring impactful issues requiring user judgment to Attention, whether already known or newly discovered. An implementation can faithfully follow the current spec while still exposing a missing expectation or an unconsidered consequence.

These are two review purposes, not a partition into known and unknown categories. A straightforward deviation can be corrected against an unambiguous agreement. But conflicting known requirements, an existing unanswered question, or a newly discovered issue may each require user judgment. The criterion for Attention is consequential impact on behavior, scope, or risk, not whether the issue was previously unknown. Passing tests does not replace either review purpose.

Now imagine a helper still uses seven days, and its tests expect seven days too. They agree with each other but conflict with REC-01. Reconciliation means correcting that drift and rerunning affected scenarios. It does not mean rewriting the agreed spec to excuse the current code. If the user actually wants a different policy, we update and confirm the affected spec first, then revise code and checks. Fixing drift against an existing agreement does not require inventing a spec change. These safeguards enforce a process; they do not guarantee that every misunderstanding or defect will be detected.

The second commitment connects directly to the four-category mental model. Attention can arise across all four categories: KK requirements may conflict; KU questions may remain unresolved; UK expectations may become explicit; and UU issues may be discovered. Keeping code faithful to a spec is necessary, but an incomplete spec can still miss what the user needs. Known unknowns are already recognized questions. Unknown knowns are expectations the user has not articulated, while unknown unknowns are issues they have not considered at all. Discovery does not stop when the first specification is agreed.

Implementation and post-implementation review can expose clues to both unknown categories. For example, a user may recognize an unstated expectation that shared files remain available to collaborators. An unfamiliar retention obligation may introduce an issue they had never considered. These are prompts for clarification, not requirements the agent is entitled to confirm on its own.

Once an unknown is surfaced, make it an explicit question, ask the user, and update the agreement from the confirmed answer before the affected work continues. Discovery turns hidden uncertainty into something discussable; user confirmation turns it into agreed intent. This is an ongoing loop, not a promise that Tandem will discover every unknown.

For the second commitment, suppose implementation exposes an unresolved question about legal retention or shared files. The agent must not quietly choose a consequential default. Tandem brings the question back to the user and pauses the work that depends on it. Clear implementation drift calls for correction; a consequential choice requires user input, whether it is new or already known.

Implementation and validation are mechanisms supporting those commitments. We validate use cases and expected outcomes across the relevant components: access stops immediately, recovery works before 30 days, and is rejected at and after the deadline. Unit tests remain useful, but passing isolated checks does not by itself establish that the user flow works.

The smaller note is intentionally different. Making alignment inspectable is our current supporting direction, and may evolve. Showing evidence, changes, and open decisions is useful, but we are not fixing that presentation as a third core contribution. Whatever form it takes, recovery evidence must not be presented as approval of the proposed interface or authorization for purge.

Intent-alignment workspace

State that this is illustrative, then point to Attention, Spec & evidence, and Meaningful changes.

This is an illustrative workspace state, not a report that we have run a real account-deletion implementation for this presentation. Its purpose is to show how the information could be organized around what the user needs to understand.

In the center, the agreed intent, specification, implementation, and evidence are connected. REC-01 still means immediate blocking of normal access, recovery before 30 days, and rejection at and after that deadline. In this illustration, the stale seven-day helper has been corrected and the scoped use-case scenarios have passed.

On the left, we have two blockers and one clue. Legal retention and shared-asset ownership remain unresolved, so permanent purge is blocked. OBS-01 is different: it is the earlier observation that the user looked for a deadline and Undo. It still awaits confirmation. A passing recovery-policy scenario does not establish that this proposed interface is wanted, implemented, or validated.

On the right, the activity is expressed as meaningful changes: the agreement was established, drift was corrected, and recovery scenarios passed. This complements the detailed execution logs, rather than asking the user to reconstruct the story from every file read and tool call.

The intended outcome is that the user can answer four questions quickly: What is settled? What changed? What evidence supports it? Where do you still need a decision from me? That is a more useful view of progress than treating all visible activity as evidence of alignment.

The two boxes at the bottom summarize the user's view. What works as agreed? In this illustration, the access and recovery flows passed their checks against the agreed policy. What needs my decision? We still need to decide which records and shared files must survive permanent deletion, and whether the interface should show a deadline and Undo. These are different questions from whether the recovery checks passed.

This brings us back to the opening tension. Use the agent's speed to discover intent with less upfront writing, then preserve confirmed agreements with less repeated coordination. The claims remain limited: Tandem is optional, the workspace is illustrative, and reduced total effort still needs to be demonstrated.

Development walkthrough / 3 of 4

Show each numbered screenshot in order. Distinguish what is visible from what the captures cannot establish.

The first image shows a distinct post-implementation review, with a checkpoint for eleven changed files. The checkpoint is evidence that review is in progress; it is not itself a successful review result.

The second image shows why this loop matters. The use cases are marked implemented, yet review has surfaced two consequential questions: what difficulty changes and how the final score is calculated. Implemented does not mean all expectations are settled or every behavior is verified.

These questions return to user Attention and the agreement. The final history capture shows a later design revision, no remaining Attention in the queue, and a skipped review because no files changed. It does not show the exact answers and does not establish that another code-changing implementation cycle occurred.

This is the Stage 2 loop in concrete form: agreement, implementation and validation, review, user Attention and decision, then back to the agreement if needed. An empty queue is not proof that there are no undiscovered issues.

Backup / Discussion / Fair questions

Q&A: Why Tandem?

If the agent can already do all this, why Tandem?

Chat is a Swiss-army knife, not a prescribed process. An agent can prototype, write specs, and review code. Tandem explores an optional, guided workflow for faster agreement, spec-first changes, and review. It also explores an AI-native IDE beyond CLI and chat alone.

How can a non-programmer judge a spec?

Use linked visual artifacts, not walls of docs. Users judge flows, examples, and outcomes. Future direction: dynamically generate views suited to GUI, CLI, or service projects.

Could the same agent repeat its own misunderstanding?

Yes. Ask the user, not just the agent. Tandem raises questions; users answer what they expect. The agent validates use cases against those answers, not only its own assumptions.

Doesn't another workflow add effort?

It does add interaction. The aim is less total effort: prototype to reach the first agreed spec, then reuse those agreements instead of repeatedly explaining and tracking them.

A direction to explore, not a settled method. The whole approach — or only parts — may be useful. Does the guidance justify its added effort?

Backup / Q&A

Backup: use these answers during discussion, not as claims that every objection is solved.

First: if the agent can already do all this, why Tandem? The agent already provides the capabilities. If direct agent use gives you what you need, there is no obligation to use Tandem. Direct prompting is a valid way to build, including for non-programmers. Experienced developers can also maintain their own specifications and validation process. Our proposal is not an exclusive coding capability; it is a way to reduce the burden of making expectations explicit and keeping development accountable to them.

Chat is a Swiss-army knife, not a prescribed process. You can ask an agent to prototype, write specifications, and review code directly. Specifications and TDD can add discipline, but maintaining that discipline is still work. Tandem explores a repeatable, optional workflow, not a capability that ordinary agents lack.

A secondary exploration is what an AI-native IDE could be beyond CLI and chat alone. Specifications, prototypes, user decisions, and validation evidence could be interactive parts of the development workspace, rather than information the user must recover from a conversation. Chat and CLI can remain useful interfaces within that environment. This is a direction to explore, not a claim that Tandem is already a complete IDE or that these surfaces are the right final design.

Think of Tandem as a first step toward guided development rather than freestyle interaction. We are not sure whether this particular combination makes sense as a whole. Some parts may help, others may need revision or removal. We want to inspire and investigate the direction, not claim that we have already found the right process or that everyone should adopt it.

That workflow aims to reach agreement faster, update and confirm the spec before implementing changed requirements or design, and review the result for consistency and consequential decisions requiring user Attention. Review can surface issues across all four knowledge categories. A speed advantage remains something to demonstrate, not something the metaphor proves.

Second: how can a non-programmer judge a spec? We should not expect them to review pages of technical prose. The spec should be as visual and concrete as possible: different views of one shared intent. A flow can show what happens after an action. A timeline can expose a boundary. A prototype can make an interaction tangible. The future direction is to generate the useful set for the project: GUI screens, CLI command examples, or service interaction sequences, for instance. The user judges outcomes they understand, not implementation details they do not.

Third: couldn't the same agent repeat its own misunderstanding? Absolutely. The same model can carry one wrong assumption through the spec, code, and checks. We do not solve that merely by asking it to inspect itself again. Tandem raises questions for the user to answer. For example: should recovery still work exactly 30 days after deletion? The user supplies the expected outcome; the agent then exercises the relevant use cases against that answer.

That distinction matters: the user's answer establishes intent; execution evidence shows whether the software meets it. Neither substitutes for the other. It is still possible to miss a question or misunderstand an answer, so this is not a guarantee of complete intent capture or perfect software.

Finally: doesn't this add effort? It does. Questions and review take time. The hypothesis is that targeted interaction, followed by reuse of the agreement, avoids more re-explanation and rework than it costs. We should evaluate that against ordinary agent use through user effort, missed expectations, rework, and time to an accepted outcome, not by counting generated artifacts.

Closing: Tandem is not necessary to generate code. Its proposed value is helping us move quickly while preserving what the user actually means. That is the idea I would like your feedback on.

Backup / Positioning / Anthropic's AI-native SDLC playbook

Aligned direction. Our emphasis.

Shared foundation: agents do more of the work; humans retain judgment; durable artifacts connect intent, implementation, and evidence.

01 / Discover expectations

Use an early runnable prototype to reveal expectations users could not readily articulate — not merely to illustrate an accepted brief.

Experience helps form the agreement. The user confirms what the prototype reveals; its behavior is not automatically the spec.

02 / Make intent understandable

Present one agreement through linked flows, timelines, and examples — different views, not separate specifications.

Usability and auditability can coexist. Visual views can sit over a versioned, machine-actionable canonical record.

Future: adapt views to GUI, CLI, or service projects.

03 / Show outcomes and open decisions

Organize progress around agreed user outcomes, supporting evidence, and what still needs a decision — not only completed tasks or passing tests.

Make the scope of confidence visible. A validated use case does not settle every expectation.

Recovery validated. Purge blocked.
Deadline / Undo UX still awaiting confirmation.

Reference: Anthropic — The AI-native SDLC playbook. It also includes human review and iterative visual design.

Backup / Related work

Backup: use this slide if asked how Tandem relates to Anthropic's playbook. Start with the overlap, not a claim of novelty.

We are strongly aligned with the AI-native SDLC direction. The playbook argues that faster coding moves the bottleneck into planning, review, and handoffs. It connects the lifecycle through durable artifacts and keeps humans accountable for decisions requiring judgment. Tandem shares that foundation.

We should also be fair about the overlap. The playbook already includes non-engineer contributors, agent-written specifications, human correction, and iterative visual design. Our proposal is not that these ideas are absent from their approach. These three points describe where we place our emphasis.

First, discover expectations through experience. Their frontend example begins with accepted intent and then iterates on a mock. We emphasize using an early runnable experience to help form the agreement itself. A user may not know to ask for a deadline or Undo until they try deleting an account. That observation is a clue to clarify, not permission to invent a requirement. The user still confirms the expected behavior.

Second, make the agreement understandable through different views. Their early handoffs are predominantly Markdown. Our proposed interface exposes the same agreement through flows, timelines, and concrete examples. That does not require abandoning a canonical record: the visual views can be backed by versioned, machine-actionable data. They are complementary representations, not separate specs that can silently disagree. Dynamically choosing the best views for GUI, CLI, or service projects remains a future direction.

Third, show progress in terms of outcomes and unresolved decisions. In our illustration, recovery is validated while purge is blocked and the deadline-display or Undo experience still awaits confirmation. That tells the user what the evidence actually supports and where their input is needed. It is more informative than a blanket statement that implementation finished or all tests passed. It does not claim that every expectation has been captured.

Our positioning is therefore a user-facing layer within an AI-native lifecycle: help people discover expectations, understand the agreement, and judge scoped evidence. The playbook covers a broader operational lifecycle, including deployment and maintenance; this presentation does not establish that Tandem covers all of it. Whether our emphasis reduces misunderstanding and total user effort remains something we need to demonstrate.

Discussion takeaway: The distinction is not more AI-generated artifacts. It is making the intent behind them easier for the user to establish, understand, and keep connected to the delivered software.
